findings.subject: pam_pwquality.so
findings.detail: pam_pwquality.so is enforced, but minlen and minclass and the four credit settings are set neither in /etc/security/pwquality.conf nor as an argument on the PAM line. The effective value then comes from libpwquality's compiled-in default, which is a property of the package build rather than of this host, is not readable from the filesystem, and has changed between releases. Setting it explicitly is worth doing for that reason alone.

findings.subject: pam_faillock.so
findings.detail: No failed-attempt counter is in the auth stack (/etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth), so an account may be guessed at without limit. sshd counts failures per connection and gives up, which makes remote brute force expensive; su, sudo and console login have no counter of their own, so an attacker who already has a shell may guess at the next account as fast as the hardware allows.

findings.subject: pam_unix.so
findings.detail: pam_unix.so accepts an empty password in 4 rules (/etc/pam.d/system-auth:5, /etc/pam.d/password-auth:5). An account whose password field in /etc/shadow is empty can then be logged into by anyone who knows its name, with no credential at all. USERS-0003 reports whether any account is currently in that state; this is the half that decides what happens when one is.

findings.subject: pam_unix.so
findings.detail: pam_unix.so hashes passwords with sha512, so a stolen /etc/shadow is expensive to attack. What is already in the file is USERS-0006's question — the algorithm applies when a password is set, not retroactively.

evidence.excerpt: password sufficient pam_unix.so try_first_pass use_authtok nullok sha512 shadow
password sufficient pam_unix.so try_first_pass use_authtok nullok sha512 shadow

findings.subject: pam_pwhistory.so
findings.detail: No password history is kept: neither pam_pwhistory.so nor pam_unix.so carries a 'remember' argument in the password stack (/etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth). A user required to change their password may set it to the one they are replacing, which makes an expiry policy a recurring inconvenience that produces no security, and makes a post-compromise forced reset a no-op for exactly the account whose old password is already known. NIST SP 800-63B would not require this control; CIS and DISA do, and the finding is LOW because of that disagreement.

findings.subject: /tmp
findings.detail: /tmp is not a separate mount: it is part of the filesystem mounted at / and inherits its options. nodev, nosuid and noexec are per-mount properties, so a directory that is merely a subdirectory of another filesystem cannot carry them — and /tmp is where anything an unprivileged account brings to the host lands, so it is the one filesystem where removing the ability to execute, to escalate through setuid and to reach a device is worth the inconvenience

evidence.excerpt: no entry for /tmp; the governing mount is / (rw,relatime)

findings.subject: /dev/shm
findings.detail: /dev/shm is a separate tmpfs mount carrying nodev, nosuid, noexec (mounted rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime).

findings.subject: /home
findings.detail: /home is not a separate mount: it is part of the filesystem mounted at / and inherits its options. nodev, nosuid and noexec are per-mount properties, so a directory that is merely a subdirectory of another filesystem cannot carry them — and home directories are writable by the people who own them, so /home is where a setuid binary or a device node an attacker leaves behind would sit — and nosuid and nodev make both inert without costing any user anything

evidence.excerpt: no entry for /home; the governing mount is / (rw,relatime)

Reverse-path filtering is enabled on all 1 non-loopback interface(s); packets with unroutable source addresses are dropped. eth0 in loose mode (value 2), which accepts a source routable via any interface — correct for asymmetric routing, weaker than strict mode.

findings.subject: fs.protected_symlinks
findings.detail: fs.protected_symlinks is 1; symlinks in world-writable sticky directories are only followed when the follower or the directory owner owns the link.

findings.subject: fs.protected_hardlinks
findings.detail: fs.protected_hardlinks is 1; a hardlink may only be created to a file the user owns or can read and write.

findings.subject: fs.protected_fifos

findings.subject: fs.protected_regular
findings.detail: fs.protected_regular is 2; the restriction covers group-writable sticky directories as well as world-writable ones.

findings.subject: kernel.perf_event_paranoid
findings.detail: kernel.perf_event_paranoid is 2; unprivileged users may not profile the kernel, take CPU-wide measurements, or read raw tracepoints.

findings.subject: kernel.core_pattern
findings.detail: kernel.core_pattern is "core", which is a relative path, so a core dump is written into the crashing process's current working directory. A process that can be induced to run in a writable directory will drop its memory — including credentials and keys — where another user can read it.
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is 0, and an interface accepts source routing only when conf.all and its own setting are both non-zero, so source-routed packets are refused on every interface.

findings.subject: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
findings.detail: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is 1; the kernel falls back to SYN cookies when a listening socket's backlog overflows.

findings.subject: sysctl configuration
findings.detail: BPF hardening is not written to this host's sysctl configuration: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is not set in any sysctl configuration file; net.core.bpf_jit_harden is not set in any sysctl configuration file. The running kernel is currently hardened — kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is 2 — so this host is protected now and will not be after the next reboot. That is the case KERNEL-0006 reports as a pass and KERNEL-0007 does not see at all, because a parameter no file mentions has nothing to drift from. This reads the sysctl configuration files, which describe what the kernel will do after the next reboot; what it is doing now is KERNEL-0006's subject, and a disagreement between the two is KERNEL-0007's.

findings.detail: 2 system account(s) (uid 1-999) have a shell that can open a session: halt, shutdown. Anyone who obtains one of these credentials gets a login rather than a refusal.
